claims.claim: Passive touch can trigger active whisker movements in mice.
claims.source: It has been noted that passive touch can trigger active whisker movements in mice (Bellavance et al., 2017; Brown and Raman, 2018; Nguyen and Kleinfeld, 2005; Ferezou et al., 2007), but this behavior has not been described in great detail yet.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Mice made active whisker protractions following the retractions induced by the air flow in 82% of stimulus trials.
claims.source: The mice made active whisker protractions following the retractions induced by the air flow in the large majority (82%) of stimulus trials (Figure 1D–E; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's behavioral data.

claims.claim: Touch-induced protraction was typically performed by all whiskers simultaneously.
claims.source: Because of the systematic full-field air-flow from the front, the touch-induced protraction was typically performed by all whiskers simultaneously (data not shown), which is in line with the presumed reflexive nature of this movement (Bellavance et al., 2017; Brown and Raman, 2018; Nguyen and Kleinfeld, 2005).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the study supported by citations to prior work on reflexive movements.

claims.claim: Touch-induced whisker protraction was followed in about half the trials (51%) by extended periods of active whisker movements during the subsequent 200 ms interval.
claims.source: Moreover, as reported previously (Ferezou et al., 2007), the touch-induced whisker protraction was followed in about half the trials (51%) by extended periods of active whisker movements during the subsequent 200 ms interval (Figure 1D; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's behavioral data, with citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Spontaneous whisking in between stimuli was relatively rare under the experimental conditions with a 2 s inter-trial interval.
claims.source: However, under our experimental conditions with a 2 s inter-trial interval, spontaneous whisking in between the stimuli was relatively rare.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the study's experimental data.

claims.claim: Spontaneous movements with an amplitude exceeding 10° were found only in 12% of the 100 trials per mouse during the 200 ms interval prior to stimulus onset.
claims.source: Across all 16 mice measured, we found spontaneous movements (with an amplitude exceeding 10°) only in 12% of the 100 trials per mouse during the 200 ms interval prior to stimulus onset.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's behavioral data.

claims.claim: Applying the air-puff from different angles produced different retractions and different subsequent protractions.
claims.source: Thus, applying the air-puff from different angles produced different retractions and different subsequent protractions, arguing against a stereotypical startle behavior that occurs independent from the stimulus conditions.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from experiments testing different stimulus conditions.

claims.claim: No distinct explorative movements linked to the puff sources were observed.
claims.source: Finally, we also did not observe distinct explorative movements linked to the puff sources, which might have suggested dominant voluntary components (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–C).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the study's behavioral data.

claims.claim: The reactive nature of the touch-induced whisker movements in the absence of characteristic signs of startle or voluntary responses indicates that the air-puff induced protraction is a reflexive movement.
claims.source: Altogether, the reactive nature of the touch-induced whisker movements in the absence of characteristic signs of startle or voluntary responses indicates that the air-puff induced protraction is indeed a reflexive movement.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claims.claim: PCs receive sensory whisker input both directly from the brainstem and indirectly from thalamo-cortical pathways.
claims.source: In line with the fact that PCs receive sensory whisker input not only directly from the brainstem but also indirectly from thalamo-cortical pathways (Figure 2F) (Kleinfeld et al., 1999; McElvain et al., 2018; Bosman et al., 2011; Brown and Raman, 2018; Kubo et al., 2018), the dynamics of their responses upon whisker stimulation are heterogeneous (Brown and Bower, 2001; Loewenstein et al., 2005; Bosman et al., 2010; Chu et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: The dynamics of PC responses upon whisker stimulation are heterogeneous.
claims.source: In line with the fact that PCs receive sensory whisker input not only directly from the brainstem but also indirectly from thalamo-cortical pathways (Figure 2F) (Kleinfeld et al., 1999; McElvain et al., 2018; Bosman et al., 2011; Brown and Raman, 2018; Kubo et al., 2018), the dynamics of their responses upon whisker stimulation are heterogeneous (Brown and Bower, 2001; Loewenstein et al., 2005; Bosman et al., 2010; Chu et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Of the 132 single-unit PCs recorded, 118 (89%) showed significant complex spike responses.
claims.source: Of the 132 single-unit PCs from which we recorded, 118 (89%) showed significant complex spike responses, albeit with large variations in latency and amplitude (Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's electrophysiological data.

claims.claim: Cluster analysis revealed that in terms of complex spike modulation PCs can be considered as two separate clusters rather than a continuous spectrum.
claims.source: Cluster analysis revealed that in terms of complex spike modulation PCs can better be considered as two separate clusters rather than a continuous spectrum (indicated by the lowest absolute BIC value for two components (437, compared to 490 and 442 for one and three components, respectively; Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the electrophysiological data.

claims.claim: 34% of PCs were classified as 'strong' complex spike responders and 66% as 'weak' responders.
claims.source: We refer to the cells of the cluster with the higher complex spike response probability as 'strong' (34%, with a peak response above 1.98%; see Materials and methods) and the other as 'weak' (66%) responders (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–F).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from cluster analysis of the electrophysiological data.

claims.claim: Of the 132 recorded PCs, 127 (96%) showed a significant simple spike response.
claims.source: Similarly, of the 132 recorded PCs 127 (96%) showed a significant simple spike response.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's electrophysiological data.

claims.claim: Simple spike responses were often bi-phasic, consisting of a period of inhibition followed by one of excitation, or vice versa.
claims.source: Simple spike responses were often bi-phasic, consisting of a period of inhibition followed by one of excitation, or vice versa (Figure 2D–E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the study's electrophysiological data.

claims.claim: The trough of the simple spike responses typically correlated in a reciprocal fashion with the peak of the complex spike responses.
claims.source: The trough of the simple spike responses typically correlated in a reciprocal fashion with the peak of the complex spike responses (Figure 2A–E; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C) (De Zeeuw et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2014; Badura et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the study's electrophysiological data, with citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Only 2 PCs out of 132 did not show any significant modulation for either complex spikes or simple spikes.
claims.source: Only 2 PCs, out of the 132, did not show any significant modulation (i.e. for neither complex spikes nor simple spikes).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's electrophysiological data.

claims.claim: Complex spike responses to whisker stimulation were especially strong in parts of crus 1 overlapping with large areas of the C2, D1 and D2 zones.
claims.source: Complex spike responses to whisker stimulation were found to be especially strong in parts of crus 1 overlapping with large areas of the C2, D1 and D2 zones (Figure 2H), whereas the primary simple spike responses were predominantly facilitating in adjacent areas in the medial and lateral parts of crus 1 and crus 2, as predicted by the overall tendency for reciprocity (Figure 2H–I; Figure 2—figure supplement 1G–H).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from anatomical mapping of electrophysiological responses.

claims.claim: Primary simple spike responses were predominantly facilitating in adjacent areas in the medial and lateral parts of crus 1 and crus 2.
claims.source: Complex spike responses to whisker stimulation were found to be especially strong in parts of crus 1 overlapping with large areas of the C2, D1 and D2 zones (Figure 2H), whereas the primary simple spike responses were predominantly facilitating in adjacent areas in the medial and lateral parts of crus 1 and crus 2, as predicted by the overall tendency for reciprocity (Figure 2H–I; Figure 2—figure supplement 1G–H).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from anatomical mapping of electrophysiological responses.

claims.claim: PCs with strong complex spike responses were situated most prominently in centro-lateral parts of crus 1.
claims.source: These experiments confirmed that the PCs with strong complex spike responses were situated most prominently in centro-lateral parts of crus 1, whereas the PCs with weak complex spike responses were predominant in adjacent areas in crus 1 and crus 2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from anatomical tracing experiments.

claims.claim: PCs with weak complex spike responses were predominant in adjacent areas in crus 1 and crus 2.
claims.source: These experiments confirmed that the PCs with strong complex spike responses were situated most prominently in centro-lateral parts of crus 1, whereas the PCs with weak complex spike responses were predominant in adjacent areas in crus 1 and crus 2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from anatomical tracing experiments.

claims.claim: Complex spikes have been reported to encode the destination of arm movements at the start of a movement.
claims.source: As complex spikes have been reported to be able to encode, at the start of a movement, the destination of arm movements (Kitazawa et al., 1998), we wondered whether a similar association could be found for whisker movements.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: During trials with a complex spike, the protraction was significantly larger than trials without a complex spike.
claims.source: It turned out that during the trials with a complex spike, the protraction was significantly larger (see Figure 3A for a single PC; Figure 3B for the population of 55 PCs of which we had electrophysiological recordings during whisker tracking and that responded to air-puff stimulation).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from analysis of the relationship between complex spikes and whisker movements.

claims.claim: The peak in complex spike activity preceded the moment of maximal difference in position by 63 ± 4 ms.
claims.source: A direct comparison between the timing of the complex spike response and the difference in whisker position between trials with and without a complex spike revealed that the peak in complex spike activity preceded the moment of maximal difference in position by 63 ± 4 ms (mean ±SEM; n = 55; Figure 3C–D).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from temporal analysis of the data.

claims.claim: The maximal difference in protraction in trials with a complex spike equaled 0.80° (median, with IQR of 2.80°; p<0.001).
claims.source: The maximal difference in protraction in trials with a complex spike equaled 0.80° (median, with IQR of 2.80°; p<0.001), whereas this was only 0.28° (0.92°) for retraction (p=0.002; Wilcoxon matched pairs tests, significant after Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons: α = 0.05/3 = 0.017) (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis of the data.

claims.claim: Trials that started with a complex spike showed bigger whisker protractions than those without a complex spike.
claims.source: These findings imply that trials that started with a complex spike showed bigger whisker protractions than those without a complex spike.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claims.claim: There was no obvious correlation between the strength of the complex spike response of any given PC and the difference in touch-induced whisker protraction in trials with and without a complex spike.
claims.source: This did not seem to be the case (R = 0.119; p=0.386; Pearson correlation; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis of the data.

claims.claim: The complex spike of any PC showing whisker-related complex spike activity could have a similar predictive power for the amplitude of the subsequent protraction.
claims.source: Thus, in general, the complex spike of any PC showing whisker-related complex spike activity could have a similar predictive power for the amplitude of the subsequent protraction.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation analysis.

claims.claim: Complex firing in the D2 zone had the strongest predictive value for increased touch-induced whisker protraction.
claims.source: Thus, complex firing in the D2 zone had the strongest predictive value for increased touch-induced whisker protraction.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the spatial analysis of PC responses.

claims.claim: Motor control can be related to the coherence of complex spike firing of adjacent PCs.
claims.source: Previous studies showed that motor control can be related to the coherence of complex spike firing of adjacent PCs (Mukamel et al., 2009; Hoogland et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Upon whisker pad stimulation, complex spike firing occurred much more often collectively in multiple PCs.
claims.source: Upon whisker pad stimulation, however, complex spike firing occurred much more often collectively in multiple PCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from two-photon calcium imaging experiments.

claims.claim: The levels of coherence increased to such strength that they were extremely unlikely to have occurred by the increase in firing frequency alone.
claims.source: The levels of coherence increased to such strength that they were extremely unlikely to have occurred by the increase in firing frequency alone (compared to a re-distribution of all events based on a Poisson distribution; Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the imaging data.

claims.claim: Firing of a single or a few PCs was the dominant mode of activity in the absence of stimulation, and this changed toward the involvement of multiple PCs upon stimulation, firing coherently.
claims.source: In other words, firing of a single or a few PCs was the dominant mode of activity in the absence of stimulation, and this changed toward the involvement of multiple PCs upon stimulation, firing coherently as can be seen in the change in distribution of coherently active PCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F–G).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from analysis of the imaging data.

claims.claim: Groups of adjacent PCs respond to whisker pad stimulation by increased complex spike firing with an enhanced level of coherence.
claims.source: We conclude that groups of adjacent PCs respond to whisker pad stimulation by increased complex spike firing with an enhanced level of coherence, which is likely to further facilitate the occurrence of bigger whisker reflexes (see above).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the imaging data.

claims.claim: In the large majority of PCs, simple spike firing is correlated with protraction and in a minority it correlates with retraction.
claims.source: The firing rate of simple spikes has been shown to correlate with whisker position: in the large majority of PCs, simple spike firing is correlated with protraction and in a minority it correlates with retraction (Brown and Raman, 2018; Chen et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: In 25 of the 56 PCs (45%), there was a positive correlation between instantaneous simple spike firing and whisker protraction that occurred relatively late during the movement, in particular between 80 and 200 ms after the start of the stimulus.
claims.source: This turned out to be the general pattern in 25 of the 56 PCs (45%) of which we had electrophysiological recordings during whisker tracking (Figure 4D). In all these 25 PCs, there was a positive correlation between instantaneous simple spike firing and whisker protraction that occurred relatively late during the movement, in particular between 80 and 200 ms after the start of the stimulus (Figure 4C–D; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C), thus well after the complex spike responses occurred (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from correlation analysis of the data.

claims.claim: In the 31 remaining PCs that did not display a significant correlation at the individual cell level, a slight yet significant negative correlation was observed at the population level.
claims.source: In the 31 remaining PCs, that is the ones that did not display a significant correlation when evaluated at the level of individual cells, we still observed a slight, yet significant, correlation at the population level. Remarkably, this correlation was slightly negative, that is possibly reflecting a correlation between simple spike firing and retraction (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from population-level correlation analysis.

claims.claim: During the touch-induced whisker reflex simple spikes predominantly correlate with whisker protraction and this correlation is maximal without a clear time lead or lag.
claims.source: We conclude that during the touch-induced whisker reflex simple spikes predominantly correlate with whisker protraction and that this correlation is maximal without a clear time lead or lag, unlike the complex spikes, the occurrence of which tended to precede the reflexive protraction.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation analysis.

claims.claim: 4 Hz stimulation of the parallel fiber inputs leads to LTP of parallel fiber to PC synapses in reduced preparations.
claims.source: We hypothesized that whisker movements might be enhanced following air-puff stimulation at 4 Hz, as this frequency has been shown to be particularly effective in inducing potentiation at the parallel fiber-to-PC synapse (Coesmans et al., 2004; D'Angelo et al., 2001; Lev-Ram et al., 2002; Ramakrishnan et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Application of 4 Hz air-puff stimulation to the whisker pad for only 20 s was sufficient to induce an increase in the maximal protraction (average increase 17.9 ± 3.9%; mean ±SEM; p<0.001; Wilcoxon-matched pairs test; n = 16 mice).
claims.source: Indeed, application of this 4 Hz air-puff stimulation to the whisker pad for only 20 s was sufficient to induce an increase in the maximal protraction (average increase 17.9 ± 3.9%; mean ±SEM; p<0.001; Wilcoxon-matched pairs test; n = 16 mice) (Figure 5A–B; Supplementary file 1B).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the training experiments.

claims.claim: The change in the amplitude of the touch-induced whisker protraction was not accompanied by any substantial change in the complex spike response to whisker pad stimulation (p=0.163; Wilcoxon matched pairs test; n = 55 PCs).
claims.source: This change in the amplitude of the touch-induced whisker protraction was not accompanied by any substantial change in the complex spike response to whisker pad stimulation (p=0.163; Wilcoxon matched pairs test; n = 55 PCs) (Figure 5C; Supplementary file 1B).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the electrophysiological data.

claims.claim: The rate of simple spike firing upon air-puff stimulation was markedly increased after 20 s of 4 Hz air-puff stimulation, especially during the first 60 ms after the air-puff (p=0.003; Wilcoxon matched pairs test; n = 55 PCs).
claims.source: However, the rate of simple spike firing upon air-puff stimulation was markedly increased after 20 s of 4 Hz air-puff stimulation. This was especially clear during the first 60 ms after the air-puff (p=0.003; Wilcoxon matched pairs test; n = 55 PCs) (Figure 5D; Supplementary file 1B).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis of the electrophysiological data.

claims.claim: The short period of 4 Hz air-puff stimulation caused an anticipation of the moment of maximal correlation between simple spike firing and whisker position.
claims.source: The short period of 4 Hz air-puff stimulation caused an anticipation of the moment of maximal correlation between simple spike firing and whisker position. Along the 45° line – thus regarding only the zero-lag correlation between simple spike firing and whisker position – this changed from 152.1 ± 18.1 ms to 90.7 ± 9.4 ms (means ± SEM); p=0.020; t = 2.664; df = 13; paired t test; n = 14 PCs) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from temporal correlation analysis.

claims.claim: The slope of the correlation between the instantaneous simple spike frequency and the whisker position remained unaltered after 4 Hz stimulation (p=0.197, t = 1.360, df = 13, n = 14, paired t test).
claims.source: The slope of the correlation between the instantaneous simple spike frequency and the whisker position remained unaltered (p=0.197, t = 1.360, df = 13, n = 14, paired t test) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–D).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis of the correlation data.

claims.claim: After induction, the simple spikes led the whisker position (pre-induction: Δtime = 0 ± 10 ms; post-induction: Δtime = 20 ± 30 ms; medians ± IQR; n = 14; p=0.001; Wilcoxon matched-pairs test).
claims.source: However, the point of maximal correlation was no longer with a zero-lag, but after induction the simple spikes led the whisker position (pre-induction: Δtime = 0 ± 10 ms; post-induction: Δtime = 20 ± 30 ms; medians ± IQR; n = 14; p=0.001; Wilcoxon matched-pairs test) (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from temporal correlation analysis.

claims.claim: Not only the simple spike rate increased, but also its relative timing to the touch-induced whisker protraction changed, now preceding the likewise increased touch-induced whisker protraction.
claims.source: Thus, not only the simple spike rate increased, but also its relative timing to the touch-induced whisker protraction changed, now preceding the likewise increased touch-induced whisker protraction.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the temporal analysis.

claims.claim: During the entrainment itself, the whisker responses as well as the complex spike and the simple spike responses to each air-puff were weakened compared to the pre-induction period.
claims.source: During the entrainment itself (i.e. during the 20 s period with 4 Hz air-puff stimulation), the whisker responses as well as the complex spike and the simple spike responses to each air-puff were weakened compared to the pre-induction period during which we used 0.5 Hz stimulation.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from comparison of responses during different stimulation frequencies.

claims.claim: The touch-induced whisker protraction decreased by 62.2% (median; IQR = 37.5%) during 4 Hz stimulation.
claims.source: More specifically, the touch-induced whisker protraction decreased by 62.2% (median; IQR = 37.5%).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the behavioral data.

claims.claim: The maximum response of the complex spikes significantly decreased from a median of 1.27% (with an IQR of 1.89%) during pre-induction to 0.52% (with an IQR of 0.43%) during induction (p<0.001; Wilcoxon matched pairs tests, n = 55 PCs).
claims.source: The maximum response of the complex spikes significantly decreased from a median of 1.27% (with an IQR of 1.89%) during pre-induction to 0.52% (with an IQR of 0.43%) during induction (p<0.001; Wilcoxon matched pairs tests, n = 55 PCs), and the average modulation of the simple spikes in the first 200 ms after the puff decreased from a median of 5.9% (with an IQR of 18.2%) during pre-induction to -0.3% (IQR = 3.13) during induction (p=0.039, Wilcoxon matched-pairs test) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis of the electrophysiological data.

claims.claim: During the 4 Hz training stage, all responses – both at the behavioral and neuronal level – diminished compared to the preceding 0.5 Hz stimulation stage.
claims.source: Thus, during the 4 Hz training stage, all responses – both at the behavioral and neuronal level – diminished compared to the preceding 0.5 Hz stimulation stage.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of responses during different stimulation frequencies.

claims.claim: Contralateral air-puff stimulation triggers a stronger protraction than ipsilateral stimulation.
claims.source: Given the correlation between instantaneous simple spike rate and whisker position described above, one would expect that contralateral air-puff stimulation – which triggers a stronger protraction (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) – also triggers a stronger simple spike response.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from experiments comparing ipsilateral and contralateral stimulation.

claims.claim: The change in maximal protraction between contralateral and ipsilateral stimulation was considerable (difference in maximal protraction: 7.30 ± 1.24° (mean ±SEM); n = 9 mice).
claims.source: The change in maximal protraction was considerable (difference in maximal protraction: 7.30 ± 1.24° (mean ±SEM); n = 9 mice) (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C; cf. Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the comparison experiments.

claims.claim: The simple spikes increased significantly more during contralateral stimulation (increase during first 60 ms after air-puff onset for contra- vs. ipsilateral stimulation: 13.7 ± 5.3%; mean ±SEM; p=0.023; t = 2.413; df = 26; paired t test; n = 27 PCs).
claims.source: However, in addition a change in simple spikes may contribute to this difference as well, as the simple spikes increased significantly more during contralateral stimulation (increase during first 60 ms after air-puff onset for contra- vs. ipsilateral stimulation: 13.7 ± 5.3%; mean ±SEM; p=0.023; t = 2.413; df = 26; paired t test; n = 27 PCs) (Figure 5—figure supplement 3E).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis of the comparison data.

claims.claim: The complex spikes were less activated during contralateral stimulation (complex spike peak response: ipsilateral: 1.40% (1.25%); contralateral: 0.71% (0.81%); medians (IQR); p<0.001; Wilcoxon matched-pairs test; n = 27 PCs).
claims.source: Instead, the complex spikes were less activated during contralateral stimulation (complex spike peak response: ipsilateral: 1.40% (1.25%); contralateral: 0.71% (0.81%); medians (IQR); p<0.001; Wilcoxon matched-pairs test; n = 27 PCs) (Figure 5—figure supplement 3D).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis of the comparison data.

claims.claim: Simple spikes modulate ongoing whisker movements rather than initiate them.
claims.source: Previously, it has been shown that simple spikes modulate ongoing whisker movements rather than initiate them (Brown and Raman, 2018; Chen et al., 2016; Proville et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: The whisker protraction was substantially bigger during the period of optogenetic stimulation (p<0.001; t = 4.411; df = 12; paired t test; n = 13 mice).
claims.source: As expected, the whisker protraction was substantially bigger during the period of optogenetic stimulation (p<0.001; t = 4.411; df = 12; paired t test; n = 13 mice; Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from optogenetic experiments.

claims.claim: Increases in simple spike firing can cause stronger whisker protraction.
claims.source: Thus, even though optogenetic stimulation of PCs can also trigger secondary feedback mechanisms that may influence the outcome (Witter et al., 2013; Chaumont et al., 2013), we conclude that increases in simple spike firing can cause stronger whisker protraction.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the optogenetic experiments, with citations to prior work on potential confounds.

claims.claim: Cerebellar plasticity is bi-directional and under control of climbing fiber activity.
claims.source: As cerebellar plasticity is bi-directional and under control of climbing fiber activity (Ohtsuki et al., 2009; Lev-Ram et al., 2003; Coesmans et al., 2004), we wanted to find out to what extent plastic changes in simple spike activity can be related to the strength of the complex spike response generated by climbing fibers.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: There was a significant negative correlation between the strength of the complex spike response before 4 Hz air-puff stimulation and the change in simple spike response following this 4 Hz stimulation (R = 0.311; p=0.021; Pearson correlation; n = 55 PCs).
claims.source: As expected, we found a significant negative correlation between the strength of the complex spike response, as measured by the peak of the PSTH before the 4 Hz air-puff stimulation, and the change in simple spike response following this 4 Hz stimulation (R = 0.311; p=0.021; Pearson correlation; n = 55 PCs) (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from correlation analysis.

claims.claim: The correlation between the frequency of complex spike firing and the change in simple spike activity after 4 Hz air-puff stimulation was present only in the weak responders.
claims.source: The correlation found between the frequency of complex spike firing and the change in simple spike activity after 4 Hz air-puff stimulation proved to be present only in the weak responders, taking the firing rate during the pre-induction and induction period into account (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from subgroup analysis of the correlation data.

claims.claim: Parallel fiber activity in the absence of climbing fiber activity promotes parallel fiber to PC LTP.
claims.source: This is again in line with the notion that parallel fiber activity in the absence of climbing fiber activity promotes parallel fiber to PC LTP (Coesmans et al., 2004; Lev-Ram et al., 2002; Ramakrishnan et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: The PCs with the strongest effect of 4 Hz air-puff stimulation on simple spike firing were mainly located in the lateral part of crus 2.
claims.source: The PCs with the strongest effect of 4 Hz air-puff stimulation on simple spike firing were mainly located in the lateral part of crus 2 (Figure 6B), posterior to the crus 1 area with the strongest complex spike responses (Figure 2H).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from anatomical mapping of the plasticity effects.

claims.claim: The lateral crus 2 area with the strongest simple spike increase matched well with the area showing the strongest correlations between simple spike firing and whisker protraction.
claims.source: We compared the location of this lateral crus 2 area to that of the PCs with the strongest correlations between simple spike firing and whisker protraction and we found these two crus 2 locations to match well (Figure 6B–C).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from comparison of anatomical maps.

claims.claim: The impact of 4 Hz air-puff stimulation on the simple spike activity of PCs with a weak complex spike response lasted at least 30 min.
claims.source: The impact of 4 Hz air-puff stimulation on the simple spike activity of PCs with a weak complex spike response lasted as long as our recordings lasted (i.e. at least 30 min), whereas that on PCs with a strong complex spike response was not detectable during this period (Figure 6D–F).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from long-term recording of PC activity.

claims.claim: The weak responders differed significantly from the strong responders in the duration of simple spike changes (weak vs. strong responders: p=0.005; F = 3.961; df = 4.424; two-way repeated measures ANOVA with Greenhouse-Geyser correction; n = 8 weak and n = 6 strong responders).
claims.source: Indeed, the weak responders differed significantly from the strong responders in this respect (weak vs. strong responders: p=0.005; F = 3.961; df = 4.424; two-way repeated measures ANOVA with Greenhouse-Geyser correction; n = 8 weak and n = 6 strong responders; Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from statistical analysis comparing subgroups.

claims.claim: The impact of the 4 Hz air-puff stimulation on touch-induced whisker protraction also lasted throughout the recording.
claims.source: Likewise, the impact of the 4 Hz air-puff stimulation on touch-induced whisker protraction also lasted throughout the recording in that the protraction sustained (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from long-term behavioral measurements.

claims.claim: Both simple spikes and whisker muscles remained affected by the 4 Hz air-puff stimulation for as long as the recordings lasted.
claims.source: Thus, both simple spikes and whisker muscles remained affected by the 4 Hz air-puff stimulation for as long as our recordings lasted.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the long-term recording data.

claims.claim: In reduced preparations, 4 Hz stimulation of the parallel fiber inputs leads to LTP of parallel fiber to PC synapses.
claims.source: In reduced preparations, 4 Hz stimulation of the parallel fiber inputs leads to LTP of parallel fiber to PC synapses (Coesmans et al., 2004; Lev-Ram et al., 2002; Ramakrishnan et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Parallel fiber LTP is inhibited by climbing fiber activity.
claims.source: At the same time, parallel fiber LTP is inhibited by climbing fiber activity (Coesmans et al., 2004; Lev-Ram et al., 2003; Ohtsuki et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

results.result: Air-puff stimulation of the whisker pad reliably evokes reflexive whisker protraction in awake mice. Mice made active whisker protractions in 82% of trials following air-puff-induced retraction, with all whiskers moving simultaneously. Spontaneous whisking was rare (12% of trials), and the movement characteristics varied with stimulus angle, indicating a reflexive rather than startle or voluntary response.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C32 provide converging behavioral evidence characterizing the touch-induced whisker movement as reflexive. The quantitative data on response frequency (C24, C28), simultaneous whisker movement (C25), angle-dependence (C29), and absence of exploratory movements (C31) collectively support the reflexive nature conclusion (C32). The experimental controls testing different stimulus conditions strengthen this interpretation.

results.result: Purkinje cells in crus 1 and crus 2 show heterogeneous responses to whisker stimulation. Of 132 recorded PCs, 89% showed significant complex spike responses and 96% showed simple spike responses. Cluster analysis revealed two populations: 34% 'strong' and 66% 'weak' complex spike responders. Strong responders were located predominantly in centro-lateral crus 1 (C2, D1, D2 zones), while weak responders were in adjacent areas of crus 1 and crus 2.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C45 present a comprehensive electrophysiological characterization with appropriate statistical analysis (cluster analysis with BIC criterion in C36) and anatomical mapping. The quantitative data on response frequencies, cluster proportions, and spatial distributions are internally consistent and supported by both electrode recordings and anatomical tracing (C44-C45). The reciprocal relationship between complex and simple spike responses (C40) aligns with established cerebellar physiology.

results.result: Complex spikes predict larger whisker protractions on a trial-by-trial basis. Trials with complex spikes showed significantly larger protraction (median 0.80°, p<0.001) than trials without. The complex spike peak preceded maximal protraction difference by 63±4 ms. This predictive relationship was similar across PCs regardless of response strength, with the strongest effect in the D2 zone.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C54 demonstrate a temporal and quantitative relationship between complex spikes and behavior with appropriate statistics (Wilcoxon tests with Bonferroni correction in C49). The temporal precedence (C48) supports a predictive rather than reactive relationship. The lack of correlation with response strength (C51-C52) and spatial specificity (C54) provide additional mechanistic insight. The analysis appropriately controls for multiple comparisons.

results.result: Whisker pad stimulation induces coherent complex spike firing across multiple Purkinje cells. Two-photon calcium imaging revealed that complex spikes occurred collectively in multiple PCs upon stimulation, with coherence levels exceeding those expected from increased firing frequency alone (Poisson distribution comparison). The dominant mode shifted from single/few PC firing at baseline to multiple coherent PC firing during stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C59 provide imaging evidence for ensemble PC activity with appropriate statistical controls (Poisson distribution comparison in C57). The shift in activity patterns (C58) is quantified and the conclusion about coherent firing (C59) follows logically from the data. However, the causal link to 'bigger whisker reflexes' in C59 is somewhat speculative as it relies on correlation with the single-trial analysis rather than direct manipulation.

results.result: Simple spike firing correlates with whisker protraction during reflexive movements. In 45% of PCs (25/56), there was a positive correlation between simple spike firing and protraction occurring 80-200 ms after stimulus onset, without clear temporal lead or lag. The remaining 31 PCs showed a slight negative correlation at the population level, possibly reflecting correlation with retraction.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C63 present correlation analysis between neural activity and behavior with clear temporal characterization. The finding of zero-lag correlation (C63) contrasts with the complex spike lead time, providing mechanistic distinction. The analysis appropriately distinguishes individual cell-level from population-level effects (C62). However, the interpretation of negative correlation as retraction-related (C62) is somewhat speculative without direct validation.

results.result: Brief 4 Hz air-puff stimulation (20 s) induces lasting enhancement of whisker protraction and simple spike firing. Maximal protraction increased by 17.9±3.9% (p<0.001, n=16 mice) without changes in complex spike responses (p=0.163). Simple spike firing increased significantly during the first 60 ms post-stimulus (p=0.003, n=55 PCs). Critically, the temporal relationship changed: simple spikes shifted from zero-lag to leading whisker position by 20±30 ms (p=0.001).
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C71 demonstrate training-induced plasticity with appropriate statistical tests and sample sizes. The dissociation between simple and complex spike changes (C66 vs C67) is important for mechanistic interpretation. The temporal shift analysis (C68, C70) provides strong evidence for a change in the functional relationship, not just magnitude. The unchanged correlation slope (C69) indicates the relationship's nature is preserved while timing changes. Statistical power appears adequate based on effect sizes and p-values.

results.result: During 4 Hz training, all responses (behavioral and neuronal) were suppressed compared to 0.5 Hz baseline. Whisker protraction decreased by 62.2% (median), complex spike peak response decreased from 1.27% to 0.52% (p<0.001), and simple spike modulation decreased from 5.9% to -0.3% (p=0.039).
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C75 document response suppression during training with appropriate statistical tests. This finding is important for distinguishing training effects from immediate responses and suggests adaptation/habituation during the induction period. The quantitative data are consistent across behavioral and neural measures. However, the functional significance of this suppression for the subsequent potentiation is not fully explained.

results.result: Contralateral whisker stimulation produces stronger protraction than ipsilateral stimulation (difference: 7.30±1.24°, n=9 mice), accompanied by greater simple spike increases (13.7±5.3% more, p=0.023, n=27 PCs) but reduced complex spike responses (ipsilateral: 1.40%, contralateral: 0.71%, p<0.001).
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C79 provide additional evidence linking simple spike activity to protraction magnitude through a different experimental manipulation. The dissociation between simple and complex spike responses (C78 vs C79) strengthens the mechanistic interpretation. The bilateral comparison is well-controlled and the statistics are appropriate. This result provides convergent evidence for the simple spike-protraction relationship established in earlier claims.

results.result: Optogenetic stimulation of Purkinje cells enhances whisker protraction. In Pcp2-Ai27 mice expressing ChR2 in PCs, whisker protraction was substantially larger during optogenetic stimulation (p<0.001, t=4.411, df=12, n=13 mice), demonstrating that increased simple spike firing can cause stronger whisker protraction.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C82 provide causal evidence through optogenetic manipulation, strengthening the correlational findings. The statistical test is appropriate and the effect is robust. However, C82 appropriately acknowledges potential confounds from secondary feedback mechanisms (citing Witter et al., 2013; Chaumont et al., 2013), which somewhat limits the directness of the causal inference. The conclusion is reasonable but should be interpreted with this caveat.

results.result: Simple spike potentiation after 4 Hz training is inversely related to complex spike response strength and anatomically localized. There was a negative correlation between pre-training complex spike strength and simple spike change (R=0.311, p=0.021, n=55 PCs), present only in weak responders. PCs with strongest potentiation were in lateral crus 2, matching areas with strongest simple spike-protraction correlation. Effects lasted at least 30 min in weak responders (p=0.005 vs strong responders) but not in strong responders.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C92 establish the relationship between complex spike activity and plasticity induction with appropriate correlation analysis and anatomical mapping. The subgroup analysis (C85) and long-term recording (C89-C90) strengthen the findings. The anatomical correspondence between plasticity sites and functional correlation sites (C88) provides important convergent evidence. The statistical comparison between weak and strong responders (C90) is appropriately conducted with repeated measures ANOVA. The parallel behavioral persistence (C91) supports the functional relevance.

results.result: Pcp2-Ppp3r1 mice lacking PP2B in Purkinje cells show no training-induced enhancement. The impact of 4 Hz stimulation on protraction was significantly less in mutants vs wild-types (p=0.044, t=2.162, df=19). Wild-types showed significant pre-post differences (p<0.001) while mutants did not (p=0.647). Simple spike potentiation was absent in mutant weak responders (genotype effect: p=0.003, F=4.361, df=4.137, n=8 WT, n=9 mutant PCs).
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C104 provide genetic evidence for the LTP mechanism with appropriate controls (littermate comparisons) and statistics. The parallel absence of behavioral and neural plasticity in mutants strengthens the mechanistic link. The statistical tests are appropriate for the comparisons. However, the modest p-value for the behavioral effect (p=0.044 in C97) suggests the effect size may be smaller than in other comparisons, though still significant. The restriction to weak responders in the neural analysis (C102) is appropriately justified by prior findings.

results.result: Pcp2-Gria3 mice lacking GluA3 AMPA receptor subunits in PCs replicate the Pcp2-Ppp3r1 phenotype. No evidence for increased protraction was found (WT vs mutant: p=0.007, Tukey's post-hoc after ANOVA p=0.001, F=9.111, df=2, n=16 WT, n=6 mutant). Simple spike potentiation was absent (WT vs mutant: p=0.004, Tukey's post-hoc after ANOVA p=0.002, F=6.681, df=2, n=35 WT, n=13 mutant PCs).
results.evaluation: Claims C106-C109 provide independent genetic confirmation with a different molecular target, strengthening the LTP hypothesis. The statistical approach (ANOVA with post-hoc tests) is appropriate for comparing multiple genotypes. The convergence of two independent genetic models (C109) substantially increases confidence in the mechanism. However, the smaller sample size for Pcp2-Gria3 mice (n=6 vs n=16 WT for behavior) may limit power, though the effects remain significant.

results.result: Baseline differences in mutant mice do not explain plasticity deficits. Pcp2-Ppp3r1 mice showed moderately reduced complex spike rate, simple spike rate, and CV2, while Pcp2-Gria3 mice showed no significant deviations. Both mutants had reduced sensory responses, but baseline touch-induced protraction amplitudes were similar across genotypes. The absence of plasticity is therefore attributed to impaired LTP rather than altered baseline firing.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C115 address important alternative explanations through systematic comparison of baseline properties. The logic is sound: if Pcp2-Gria3 mice lack baseline firing abnormalities (C111) but still show plasticity deficits, the deficit is more likely due to the specific LTP impairment. The similar baseline protraction amplitudes (C114) rule out floor/ceiling effects. The conclusion (C115) appropriately integrates these control analyses. This strengthens the mechanistic interpretation of the genetic experiments.

results.result: The study establishes that parallel fiber to PC LTP underlies whisker reflex adaptation through increased simple spike activity. Before training, simple spikes correlated with whisker position without lead/lag. After training, both were enhanced with spikes leading behavior. Increased activity was prominent in cells with low complex spike response (predominantly crus 2). Two independent LTP-deficient mouse lines showed no behavioral or neural changes, demonstrating that LTP induction is required for both the neural and behavioral plasticity.
results.evaluation: This result integrates the major findings (C2-C3, C116-C119) with the mechanistic evidence from genetic models (C4, C22, C137). The convergence of correlational, optogenetic, and genetic loss-of-function evidence provides strong support for the LTP mechanism. The spatial specificity (C5, C118) and temporal dynamics (C3, C121) are well-characterized. The use of two independent genetic models substantially strengthens causal inference. The logic connecting induction mechanism (LTP) to expression mechanism (increased simple spikes) is sound and well-supported by the data.

results.result: Training changes the functional role of simple spikes from representing ongoing movement to providing instructive motor signals. Under baseline conditions, simple spikes correlated with protraction without temporal lead/lag, suggesting representation of ongoing movement. After 4 Hz training, simple spikes preceded whisker movement and predicted protraction magnitude. Optogenetic experiments confirmed that increased simple spike firing can promote protraction.
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C131 establish a functional transformation in simple spike signaling with appropriate temporal analysis and causal validation. The interpretation of zero-lag as 'ongoing movement' representation (C127) versus lead time as 'instructive signal' (C129) is reasonable though somewhat inferential. The optogenetic confirmation (C130) strengthens the causal interpretation. The integration with prior work (C131) appropriately contextualizes the findings. The conclusion is well-supported though the distinction between 'representation' and 'instruction' could benefit from additional mechanistic detail.

results.result: Purkinje cells with strong vs. weak complex spike responses play different functional roles. Strong responders (centro-lateral crus 1, D2 zone) do not show simple spike potentiation after training but may dynamically enhance reflexive protraction through coherent complex spike firing during single trials. Weak responders (medial crus 1, crus 2) show simple spike potentiation after training, with weak complex spike responses acting as a permissive gate for LTP induction.
results.evaluation: Claims C150-C158 synthesize anatomical, physiological, and plasticity data to propose distinct functional roles for PC subpopulations. The evidence for differential plasticity (C152-C153) is strong. The proposal that strong responders use coherent complex spikes for dynamic control (C154) is supported by the imaging data but somewhat speculative regarding mechanism. The permissive gate interpretation (C152) aligns with established LTP theory (appropriately cited). The integration is logical though some aspects (particularly C154) involve inference beyond direct evidence.

results.result: The introduction establishes the context for studying cerebellar plasticity in whisker reflex adaptation. Active touch is important across species, sensory activation can provoke reflexes that require adaptive control, and cerebellar plasticity likely contributes to this adaptation. While LTD has been emphasized historically, LTP may also be relevant, and different plasticity mechanisms may dominate different forms of learning. The role of increased simple spike activity in learning expression remains unclear.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C18 provide appropriate background context with extensive citations to prior work. These are primarily literature review claims establishing the rationale for the study. C18 correctly identifies a knowledge gap that the study addresses. The claims are well-supported by citations and represent accurate characterizations of the field. These are contextual rather than novel findings.

results.result: The study developed a novel whisker training paradigm using 4 Hz air-puff stimulation, predicted to induce cerebellar cortical plasticity and increase simple spike activity. The paradigm successfully enhanced touch-induced whisker protraction and PC simple spike firing for tens of minutes, with both changes absent in two LTP-deficient mouse lines.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C23 describe the experimental approach and summarize key findings. The paradigm design is justified by prior work on LTP induction frequencies (C19, C64). The successful induction of lasting changes (C20-C21) and their absence in genetic models (C22) are well-documented in the detailed results. These claims accurately summarize the experimental strategy and main findings.

results.result: The discussion contextualizes findings within established cerebellar physiology and circuitry. PCs receive heterogeneous whisker input from multiple pathways, simple spikes can modulate ongoing movements, cerebellar plasticity is bidirectional and controlled by climbing fibers, and 4 Hz stimulation induces LTP in reduced preparations. Different plasticity forms may dominate different learning types depending on downstream circuitry requirements. The whisker control circuitry likely involves trigemino-facial loops modulated by cerebellar nuclei via inhibitory reticular formation projections.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C149 (discussion-related) integrate the current findings with extensive prior literature. The anatomical and physiological context (C33-C34, C122-C123, C144-C147) is well-supported by citations. The mechanistic framework linking plasticity type to circuit requirements (C140-C143, C148-C149) is logical and appropriately cited. The speculation about specific circuit pathways (C145-C146) is clearly identified as such. These claims appropriately contextualize the findings without overstating conclusions.

results.result: Despite lacking LTP, Pcp2-Ppp3r1 mice retained a correlation between complex spike frequency during induction and simple spike changes (R=0.489, p=0.013), possibly reflecting other intact plasticity forms. This correlation pattern, along with other findings, strengthens the hypothesis that parallel fiber to PC LTP is a main mechanism underlying the observed long-term changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C103 and C105 address residual plasticity in mutants and integrate the correlational evidence. The persistence of some correlation in mutants (C103) is appropriately interpreted as potentially reflecting other plasticity mechanisms (citing prior work showing multiple plasticity forms in these mice). The overall conclusion (C105) appropriately integrates multiple lines of evidence while acknowledging LTP as 'one of the main mechanisms' rather than the sole mechanism. This nuanced interpretation is well-supported.
